title: Tshechu
standfirst: Annual festivals held in dzong courtyards on the tenth day of a lunar month, honouring Guru Rinpoche.
body: Masked cham dances, a giant thongdrel unrolled at dawn, and the whole valley in its finest dress. Paro Tshechu falls in spring, Thimphu Tshechu in September.

title: Dzongs
standfirst: Fortress-monasteries that hold both the district administration and the monastic body.
body: Whitewashed walls, a central utse tower, and windows framed in painted timber.

title: Textiles
standfirst: Weaving is one of the thirteen traditional arts.
body: A kera, the woven belt that fastens the kira, carries patterns particular to its valley and its weaver.

title: Jomzo and the crafts
standfirst: Zorig Chusum, the thirteen arts: painting, sculpture, casting, woodwork, weaving and more.
body: Jomzo shapes clay, copper and gold into sacred images, and the workshops are open — you can stand at the bench and watch a figure come up out of the clay.

title: Gross National Happiness
standfirst: Bhutan measures progress by well-being, culture, environment and good governance rather than output alone.
body: It is the only carbon-negative country in the world, and the constitution requires that sixty per cent of it stay under forest.

title: Kira and gho
standfirst: National dress worn daily: the kira for women, the gho for men, with a kabney or rachu scarf added inside dzongs and temples.

title: Archery and khuru
standfirst: Datse is the national sport and it is played everywhere, over 145 m, with singing and dancing from the team at the far end when a shot lands.
body: Khuru is its winter cousin: weighted darts thrown twenty metres at a small board.

title: At the table
standfirst: Red rice, and chilli treated as a vegetable rather than a spice.
body: Ema datshi — chillies and cheese — is the national dish. Every meal on our journeys is included, and there is always something mild alongside.
